name: AutoUE
summary: Coordinates agents to build Unreal scenes, gameplay code, interactions, and playtests.
detail: A research pipeline for turning a game description into Unreal Engine scenes and C++ gameplay. Its public implementation includes setup instructions, a demonstration video, and a linked dataset of generated games and assets. Reproduction requires Unreal integrations and external model services. The video demonstrates outputs; it is not a hosted playable game. Static inspection of the pinned evaluation dispatcher shows movement commands skipped and interaction handlers called directly; completion of that script path alone does not establish player navigation success.

tutorial.note: Author instructions for dependencies, service credentials, and running the Unreal generation pipeline.

demo.note: Recorded demonstrations of generated Unreal games; no public browser-playable build verified.

source.label: Pipeline source
source.note: Public framework implementation; engine setup, model services, and dataset assets remain separate requirements.

name: UniGen
summary: Plans Unity prototypes, generates scripts, assembles scenes, and supports iterative debugging.
detail: A multi-agent research workflow for Unity game creation from natural-language descriptions. The repository publishes its Python pipeline and model connector, with installation guidance and a recorded demonstration. Unity and a model-service account are required. Public pipeline code is available, but a hosted playable build and complete downloadable versions of the benchmark games were not verified.

tutorial.label: Installation and usage
tutorial.note: README covers prerequisites and the local Unity generation workflow; review paths and project setup before running.

demo.note: Author-linked demonstration video, not a browser-playable game.

source.note: Published generator implementation and prompts; this is not a complete release of every benchmark game.

name: Regression Games
summary: Provides a public Unity SDK for gameplay recording, input replay, and regression-test reference workflows.
detail: The public Unity SDK combines gameplay recording, state inspection, input playback, bot logic, and validation workflows. Its official first-test tutorial and Boss Room UI-testing project remain available in GitHub repositories. Treat this as a reference integration: the old documentation domain was unreachable during review, and current hosted-service availability and maintenance were not confirmed. SDK source is public; check compatibility and service requirements before adopting it.

tutorial.note: Official first-test walkthrough preserved in the documentation repository. The former live documentation domain was unreachable during review.

name: modl.ai
summary: Uses visual agents and natural-language tasks to test uploaded game builds.
detail: The current commercial service observes screens and sends simulated inputs without requiring an engine SDK. Teams upload a build, describe test tasks, and review captured sessions and bug reports. Its stated coverage includes Android and desktop; timing-critical gameplay remains limited. The vendor also describes game-specific model training using test-run data; SDK-free does not mean no game-specific preparation. The current product differs from older SDK-based documentation. Public self-service gameplay, complete product source, and an independent hands-on tutorial were not verified.

tutorial.label: Workflow overview
tutorial.note: Official upload, task-definition, and reporting overview; detailed onboarding is provided through the service.

demo.note: Commercial demonstration by arrangement; this is not a public playable game or instant sandbox.

source.label: Full product source unavailable
source.note: No complete source release for the current hosted testing product was verified; older public samples are not its backend.

name: Convai
summary: Adds conversational NPCs with speech, memory, emotion, and in-scene actions.
detail: Convai connects game characters to runtime conversation and behavior services through engine integrations. Its Unity guides cover installation, sample scenes, and character setup; public Unreal SDK source is also available. Browser experiences require an account. This provides AI behavior inside an existing game, rather than generating a complete game. Public SDKs do not include the full hosted AI service.
